titre: The Booklet the French Worker Does Not Keep for Himself
accroche: In France, from 1803, a booklet stamped by the authorities is required to move from one town to another. Until 1854, it is the employer who keeps it, not the worker.
contenu_vulgarise:
Paris, April 12, 1803, 22 germinal an XI. The Consulate requires every worker employed in manufactories and workshops to hold a booklet (livret ouvrier), issued by the mayor of his town. The document carries his name, age, place of birth, trade, and the name of the employer he works for. Without it, he cannot legally travel from one city to another to look for work.

## A Booklet Kept by the Employer, Not the Worker

The text presents it plainly as a measure “protecting the commitments between workers and those who employ them,” guaranteeing, in its own words, “workshops against desertion.” In practice, it is the employer who keeps the booklet for the entire length of the engagement. Until 1851, a worker who owes his employer money can be refused its return; a law of May 14, 1851 abolishes this retention for debt, but keeps the one aimed at an unfinished engagement, so that a worker who wants to leave before his contract ends may still find himself without the document that would legally allow him to work elsewhere. Interior Minister Chaptal, who sponsors the text, presents it as a way to “keep good order” and to protect the “good of industry.” A worker who travels without having his booklet stamped risks, under the terms of the implementing order of December 1, 1803, being treated as a vagrant.

## What Practice Eventually Corrected, Very Slowly

This equation has a limit, however, which the Cour de cassation (France's highest court of ordinary law) eventually acknowledges: in a ruling of July 9, 1829, it holds it inapplicable. The harshest lever of the 1803 law thus loses most of its force as early as 1829, though the booklet itself does not disappear. It takes the law of June 22, 1854 for a reform finally to place the document in the worker's hands rather than his employer's, and July 2, 1890 for a law, debated since a 1881 proposal, to abolish the system entirely. Some departments nonetheless keep issuing it until 1939: prefectural circulars addressed to mayors still attest to this in the Nord.

A document designed to prove the worker's loyalty to his employer ended up documenting, in spite of itself, an entire career: the jobs held, their duration, the breaks. A use that a commission of inquiry had already glimpsed in 1868, when it considered turning the compulsory booklet into a simple optional certificate, without success. The question of what a professional document should reveal about a working life has never really stopped being asked since.

repere.texte: The order of 9 frimaire an XII (December 1, 1803) treats a worker without a stamped booklet as a vagrant. The Cour de cassation holds this equation inapplicable in a ruling of July 9, 1829, though the booklet remains compulsory until 1890.
repere.source: Order of 9 frimaire an XII (December 1, 1803) and Cour de cassation ruling of July 9, 1829, cited by the Arles municipal archives

carte.punch: For half a century, the booklet that proves who you are stays in your boss's pocket
carte.idee: In 1803, France imposes a compulsory workers' booklet for any travel. Until 1854, this document stays in the employer's hands, not the worker's, so he cannot leave freely. It is not abolished until 1890, and is still issued elsewhere until 1939.

quiz.question: What does the reform of June 22, 1854 change in how the French workers' booklet works?
choix: It ends the booklet requirement for workers in workshops of fewer than twenty employees
It replaces the criminal charge of vagrancy with a simple administrative fine
It extends the booklet requirement to farm workers, previously exempt from the document
It moves custody of the booklet from the employer to the worker himself for the length of his engagement
quiz.explication: Until 1854, the employer kept the booklet throughout the engagement, which limited the worker's freedom to leave. The law of June 22, 1854 puts it back in the worker's hands, without touching either the requirement to hold the document or its abolition, which will not come until 1890.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the order of December 1, 1803, what does a worker who travels without having his booklet stamped risk?
choix: Having to pay a tax in every town he passes through
Having his booklet confiscated for life by his employer
Being sent back under escort to his hometown
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The order of 9 frimaire an XII (1803) treats a worker without a stamped booklet as a vagrant, a classification the Cour de cassation will hold inapplicable in 1829.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Cour de cassation hold in its ruling of July 9, 1829 regarding the workers' booklet?
choix: That custody of the booklet should go to the worker rather than the employer
That the workers' booklet violates the freedom of movement guaranteed by law
That treating a worker without a stamped booklet as a vagrant is inapplicable
That the law of 22 germinal an XI is repealed with immediate effect
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The ruling of July 9, 1829 holds the equation with vagrancy inapplicable, without repealing either the booklet or the 1803 law, which remain in force until 1890.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What exactly does the law of May 14, 1851 change in the workers' booklet system?
choix: It transfers custody of the booklet to the worker, as the 1854 law will do
It introduces retention of the booklet for debt, previously unknown to the law
It abolishes all retention of the booklet, whatever the reason given
It abolishes retention for debt, but keeps it for an unfinished engagement
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The law of May 14, 1851 ends retention for unpaid debt but leaves in place the retention aimed at an unfinished engagement, unlike the transfer of custody of 1854.
